page_text.title: Our tea shop is ready
page_text.subtitle: Count the cups. Does every friend have a cup?

elements.text:
Aishatu: Four friends and four cups!
Grace: Each friend has a cup.
Adamu: Everyone is included.
John: We solved the puzzle.
Mrs Binta: Now your pretend tea shop can open.

A fresh try. Work on your own.
Ask an adult to name a number from one to five.
Make that many cups or counters at the table.

Ask the adult to mix numeral cards from one to five.
Point to the numeral the adult says.
Now the adult points to a mixed card. Say its number.
Workbook: A fresh counting try. The adult chooses the numbers.

page_text.title: A fresh counting try
page_text.subtitle: An adult reads these instructions. Try before getting help.

elements.text:
Ask an adult to say a number from one to five.
Make that many large objects at the table.
Count once to check.

Ask the adult to say another number.
Draw that many circles in the large box.

Point to the numeral the adult says.
Then the adult points to a mixed card.
Say its number. Try a different order next.

page_text.subtitle: Match one object to one object to compare the sets.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: I draw a line from one top to one top. Each top can have only one partner.

Two tops in the lower set have no partner.
Four is more than two. Two is fewer than four.
I circle the whole set with more.

Adamu: The long row must have more!
Mr Aliyu: Let us match and check.
Use your finger to match each top in the upper row to a different top below. Does every top have a partner? Tell a partner.
Workbook: Sort and match.

page_text.title: Sort and match
page_text.subtitle: Watch Mr Aliyu first. You may mark this workbook.

elements.text:
Mr Aliyu circled one leaf. Circle the other leaf.
Leave the tops without circles.
Mix real leaves and tops at the table. Sort them into two groups. Count each group. Tell your partner the rule.
Draw one line from each top in the upper row to a different top below. Does every top have a partner?
Tell your partner: more, fewer, or the same number?

MATHS WITH FRIENDS
PRIMARY ONE / TEXTBOOK
CHAPTER THREE / ZERO MEANS NONE
Remember and explain
Remember what Mrs Binta showed before looking back.
Read together. Keep this textbook reusable.
Put all 3 tops away. How many remain?
Use three real counters and a storage box.
Write how many are left in your exercise book.
Say the word for 0.
Why does an empty basket have 0 oranges?
Tell a partner or show your answer with an empty container.
John: Give me thinking time before a hint.
Tell or show how you know a tray is empty.
Need help? Put one counter in a tray. Move it into a box with an adult. Look
inside the tray. Say how many are left. Match the empty tray to 0.
Then try a different tray with two counters. Put both away. Say and write how
many are left on your own paper.
Workbook: Put away and explain. Move real counters as well.

page_text.title: The game is packed away
page_text.subtitle: Use our three real game counters. Move them from the mat into the storage box.

elements.text:
Adamu: We take turns moving every top into the box.
Grace: I check the mat. No tops are left.
John: We can record none with zero.
Aishatu: Now I can close the box and start my next game!
Game mat
Storage box

Mrs Binta: Zero tops on the mat. Three tops safely stored.
Check your real mat is empty before you close the box.

A fresh try. Work on your own.
An adult sets out three trays. One is empty.
Point to the tray with no counters. Write how many it holds in your exercise book.

Ask the adult to mix cards 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Point to the numeral the adult names.
Now name each card the adult points to. Wait for your turn.
Cover all cards, earlier answers and numerals. Write zero from memory.
Workbook: A fresh zero try. An adult prepares the trays and cards.

page_text.title: Say it. Make it. Write it.
page_text.subtitle: Try together before working on your own.

elements.text:
Mrs Binta: Put one top on a tray. Move it into the box.
Adamu: I will wait for my turn to check inside.
Say how many tops are left. Point to the numeral for none.

Mrs Binta: Watch me write zero. Start at the top.
Go left, down, around and up. Close the loop.
Start

Grace: I will make one neat loop.
Air-write with Mrs Binta. Then write 0 on your own paper. Try again if the loop stays open.
Watch an empty-box drawing. Mrs Binta draws the outline. She leaves the inside empty. Then draw your own empty box on paper.
This box has nothing drawn inside.

Say the order together: 0, 1, 2, 3.
Show none, one, two and three real tops as you say each number.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: These are four different numerals. Keep the top of your paper the same way up. Do not turn a 6 over to make a 9.

Start near the top. Curve down and around.
Close the loop at the bottom.

Start at the top left. Draw across to the right.
Slant down to the left.

Start near the top. Make a small loop,
then a lower loop. Join them neatly.

Make the loop at the top first.
Then draw the downstroke on the right.

Grace: A smudge hid my loop. I can try again.
Trace, cover the model, then write on your own paper.

page_text.title: Tens and ones have places
page_text.subtitle: Ones are also called units. A bundle of ten is one ten.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: I put one ten on the left and four loose ones on the right. Count the ones in the bundle, then the loose ones.
one ten
four ones
14 fourteen
Tens
Ones

John: I thought the 4 meant four tens.
Mrs Binta: Build it and check the places.
John: Now I see it: one ten and four ones. Fourteen!
Try together: make one ten and three ones. Count all the strips. Read 13: thirteen.

page_text.title: Remember, explain and check
page_text.subtitle: Remember what Mrs Binta showed before looking back.

elements.text:
How can you check that a bundle is really one ten?
Tell or show your partner before getting a hint.

Choose a number from eleven to nineteen.
Write it in your exercise book. Build it with real strips.
Record its tens and ones. Explain how they match your number.

Adamu: I will check a bundle, then give my partner a turn.
Grace: We can open it and count the ones inside.

Need help? With an adult, count nine strips. Add one more and count them all. Tie these ten as one bundle.
Open it and check again. Then an adult gives you a new small set to bundle and record on your own paper.

For writing, practise the digits in their places. Cover the model and earlier answers before a new try.
Workbook: Make your own number.

page_text.title: Ten ones make one ten
page_text.subtitle: Watch Mrs Binta. Count each paper strip once.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Here are ten loose strips. I move each one as I count. The last number is ten.
10 ten

Mrs Binta: I put a band around these same ten strips.
They make one bundle of ten. No strips are added or lost.

one ten
Ten ones are still inside the bundle.

Try together with real strips. Count ten. Bundle them.
Open the bundle and count again. There are still ten.
Adamu: I can check each strip once.

elements.text:
Count the strips below. Make the same number with real strips.
Put a band around them. Open and count again.
How many ones are in your bundle? Write the number.

Now make two real bundles of ten. Count all the ones.
Write the total. Tell a partner how many tens and loose ones.

page_text.subtitle: Take several short turns. Work through each number before moving on.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Build 89: 8 tens and nine ones. Add one loose strip. Count the ten loose ones. Tie them as a new ten. Now there are 9 tens and no loose ones: 90, ninety. Open the new bundle to check. Count 88, 89, 90, 91.
90 ninety: 9 tens and 0 ones
94 ninety-four: 9 tens and 4 ones
99 ninety-nine: 9 tens and 9 ones
Watch, then join in. 90 ninety, 91 ninety-one, 92 ninety-two, 93 ninety-three, 94 ninety-four, 95 ninety-five, 96 ninety-six, 97 ninety-seven, 98 ninety-eight, 99 ninety-nine.
For EACH number: watch Mr Aliyu build and write it. Build and say it together; air-write, then copy on paper. Mix cards and read together. Workbook: Ninety to ninety-nine.

page_text.title: Remember and repair
page_text.subtitle: Recall first. Get help after your own try.

elements.text: How do ten loose ones become another ten? Explain or show it without looking back. Choose a number from 21 to 99. Build it. Record its tens and ones in your exercise book. Read its whole name.

Aishatu: I will let my partner finish before I check. A bundle must have ten!
John: I can explain a number in both places.
Need help? With an adult, make 19. Add one, count and tie the ten loose ones. Open the new ten and count it again. Make 29 and repeat. Then try a NEW number without help.

For a name error, build thirteen and thirty side by side. Say each name. For reversed digits, point to tens on the left and loose ones on the right. Copy once, cover it, then write a fresh spoken number.
Workbook: Remember and repair, or use an exercise book.

elements.text:
Mr Aliyu: Make the three labels we needed: forty-six, eighty-one and ninety-three.
Adamu: I write 46 and give Grace a turn.
Grace: I write 81. This time I check both places.
John: I write 93 after thinking it through.
Aishatu: I check the bundles and attach the labels to my three boxes.

46 four tens, six ones
81 eight tens, one one
93 nine tens, three ones
Build each label with real strips. Check ten in every bundle. Match each written label to the spoken name. Attach 46, 81 and 93 to three different boxes. Our game boxes now have the correct labels.
A fresh try. Use new real sets, shuffled cards and spoken numbers from the adult list. Count, build, read, recognise and write separately. Keep the answer list hidden.

page_text.title: Bring back what we know
page_text.subtitle: Build first. Say the name. Write in your workbook or exercise book.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Touch and count these strips. A tied bundle has ten separate strips. The band is not a strip.
One ten and four ones: 14, fourteen. The left digit tells the tens. The right digit tells the loose ones.
Watch me write 14: first 1, then 4 beside it. Copy on paper. Cover it and try again.
Together, count ten loose strips, tie them, then open and count again. Make twenty with two checked bundles. Zero loose ones means 0 in the ones place.
Now try alone: count a real set of seven; build twelve and twenty. Read shuffled cards 5, 19, 2, 10, 16. Copy 12, then cover every model and your writing. An adult says a new number to write.
Workbook: Ready for bigger numbers. Ask for help before moving on.

page_text.title: Hear the whole name
page_text.subtitle: Listen, build and check. The word ending can change the number.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Thirteen is one ten and three ones. Thirty is three tens and no loose ones. Listen: thirTEEN, THIRty. Build both, not just the first digit.
13 thirteen
30 thirty
Together build and say: fourteen / forty; fifteen / fifty; sixteen / sixty; seventeen / seventy; eighteen / eighty; nineteen / ninety. Count the tens and ones. Forty has no letter u.

Grace: I said sixty when I saw 16. I will look at both places and try again.
Adamu: I will wait, then ask you a different pair.
Adult: say one name from each pair. Children point to mixed cards, then build to check.

page_text.title: Write places and count on
page_text.subtitle: Watch Mr Aliyu. Then try together.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: In 27, 28, __, I say twenty-seven, twenty-eight, twenty-nine. Each next number has one more. I write 29 in the gap.
Together: 48, 49, __, __. Build 49. Add one, tie the ten loose strips, then add one more. Say fifty, fifty-one. Write 50, 51 on paper.
Mr Aliyu: I build 72 with seven bundles and two loose strips. I write: 7 tens and 2 ones. Together build 84 and record its tens and ones.
Mr Aliyu: To write 31 to 33, include both ends: 31, 32, 33. Together say and write 62 to 65. Keep the order. Check each next number has one more.
Use real strips and your exercise book, or extra workbook space. Say each whole number before you record it. Check your partner after both have tried.

page_text.title: Bring back what we know
page_text.subtitle: Build first. Say the name. Write in your workbook or exercise book.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Touch and count these strips. A tied bundle has ten separate strips. The band is not a strip.
One ten and four ones: 14, fourteen. The left digit tells the tens. The right digit tells the loose ones.
Watch me write 14: first 1, then 4 beside it. Copy on paper. Cover it and try again.
Together, count ten loose strips, tie them, then open and count again. Make twenty with two checked bundles. Zero loose ones means 0 in the ones place.
Now try alone: count a real set of seven; build twelve and twenty. Read shuffled cards 5, 19, 2, 10, 16. Copy 12, then cover every model and your writing. An adult says a new number to write.
Workbook: Ready for bigger numbers. Ask for help before moving on.

page_text.subtitle: An adult reads aloud. Use real strips. Write here.

elements.text: Count seven real strips. Record how many.
Build twelve, then twenty. Draw your bundles and loose ones.
Read each card the adult shows. Then point to the card the adult names. These are different checks.
Copy 12 here. Cover it and all earlier answers. Write the new number your adult says in the lower space.

page_text.title: Remember and repair
page_text.subtitle: Recall first. Get help after your own try.

elements.text: How do ten loose ones become another ten? Explain or show it without looking back. Choose a number from 21 to 99. Build it. Record its tens and ones in your exercise book. Read its whole name.

Aishatu: I will let my partner finish before I check. A bundle must have ten!
John: I can explain a number in both places.
Need help? With an adult, make 19. Add one, count and tie the ten loose ones. Open the new ten and count it again. Make 29 and repeat. Then try a NEW number without help.

For a name error, build thirteen and thirty side by side. Say each name. For reversed digits, point to tens on the left and loose ones on the right. Copy once, cover it, then write a fresh spoken number.
Workbook: Remember and repair, or use an exercise book.

elements.text: How do ten loose ones become another ten? Explain or show it without looking back. Choose a number from 21 to 99. Build it. Record its tens and ones in your exercise book. Read its whole name.

Aishatu: I will let my partner finish before I check. A bundle must have ten!
John: I can explain a number in both places.
Need help? With an adult, make 19. Add one, count and tie the ten loose ones. Open the new ten and count it again. Make 29 and repeat. Then try a NEW number without help.

For a name error, build thirteen and thirty side by side. Say each name. For reversed digits, point to tens on the left and loose ones on the right. Copy once, cover it, then write a fresh spoken number.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Watch me draw a rectangle on paper. I mark the middle of the top and bottom edges. I join the marks with a straight line. This makes two equal halves.
Use a folded paper edge to find the middle. Check by folding the two parts onto each other.
Watch me draw a square. I draw one line through the middle from top to bottom, then another from side to side. I count four equal parts. I shade just one.

Grace: A smudge crossed my line. I will try again on spare paper.
Mrs Binta: Neatness helps us see the parts. You can point and explain too.
Try together on paper: draw the rectangle, then the square. Check before shading.

elements.text: Need help? Work with Mrs Binta and one small rectangle. Match the edges and fold. Open. Refold and check that the two parts fit. Touch one part and say "a half".

Count the parts.
Check the same amount.
Name one part.
For quarters, use a square. Fold in half and then in half the other way. Open and touch four equal parts. Shade one on paper. An adult can hold the paper steady while you choose the folds.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Watch me turn a square without changing its pieces. In the tilted square, four equal triangles meet in the middle. One shaded triangle is a quarter.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: This complete sheet is one whole. Watch me bring one short edge exactly onto the other. Press the fold. Open the sheet.
The line shows the fold. The two pieces cover the same amount of paper. Fold again to check that they fit exactly on each other. Equal means the same amount of space here.
Each part is a half of the whole. Two equal halves make the whole. I shade one part on my paper: one half is shaded.
Try together. Take a rectangle of scrap paper. Match its short edges, fold and open. Touch each half. Say, "Two equal parts." Turn the sheet. Is each part still a half?
Grace: Turning the sheet changes its direction. It does not change the amount of paper in each half. Keep your folded sheet for the next turn.

elements.text: For help, fold a scrap rectangle with an adult. Match the edges. Open and check the equal halves. Fold a square twice in different directions. Open and touch one quarter.
Now work alone with new scrap paper. Fold a tall rectangle into equal halves. Fold a new square into equal quarters. Point to one part of each. Say its name and explain how you checked.
Draw your new folds here, or keep your folded papers with this workbook. An adult may record your explanation.
If ready, show a different way to make equal halves of a square on spare paper.

page_text.title: Turn it and name the part
page_text.subtitle: Read together. Say, point or use your workbook or exercise book.

elements.text: Mrs Binta: Watch me turn a square without changing its pieces. In the tilted square, four equal triangles meet in the middle. One shaded triangle is a quarter.
The paper orange model also has two equal parts. One part is a half. It is paper, not food. Fold a round paper model through its centre to check the matching halves.
Say together: a half is one of two equal parts; a quarter is one of four equal parts. Shape and direction may change. Equal amounts still matter.
Mrs Binta: Now we can read short names. 1/2 is read "one half": one of two equal parts. 1/4 is read "one quarter": one of four equal parts. Say the words as I point. You may answer in words.

page_text.title: Teach, observe and revisit
page_text.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text: Suggested sessions: TB1-2 concrete joining; TB3 signs and equality; TB4 three sets; TB5 drawing; TB6 / WB2-3 independent tasks; TB7 help; TB8 and WB6 fresh checks. This is flexible editorial pacing, not an official timetable.

Read directions aloud. Use large safe counters or paper circles. Keep all materials reachable for seated participation. Allow touch, pointing, speech and drawing. Model the move into one row; do not introduce counting-on, carrying or totals through eighteen here.

Observe: Does the child preserve all objects, count each once, distinguish the separate sets from the total and read the entire number sentence? If a child counts a set twice, return to 1+1, moving each counter once into one row. Then use the new 2+1 recheck (TB7 / WB4). If equals is treated as an answer arrow, build 3 and 2+1 side by side and read 3=2+1.

Delayed recall, next session: Without showing earlier answers, ask the child to join two and two counters and record the total. Then join one, one and two. Ask whether 4=2+2 is true and why. Answers: 4; 4; yes, both sides have value 4. Record whether the child worked independently or with support.
Do not infer mastery from copied numerals. Return to concrete objects when needed.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Watch me draw one dot for each top. First I draw one dot, then one more. I count both dots. I write the total.
Dots can stand for books too. Watch: two books and one more book make three books. I draw two dots and then one dot.

2 + 1 = 3
Three books.
Try together. On the workbook page "Try with Mr Aliyu" or in your exercise book, draw one dot and two more dots. Count them all. Write the total.

elements.text:
Your turn: Put the original two stall tops and one top on a reachable table. Move them into one tray. Touch each once and say the total. Then read the ending.
Grace: I keep them in a neat row.
John: Three tops altogether!
Aishatu: Waiting helped us check.
Adamu: All four friends can take turns with our three tops.
The same two tops and one top from the start are here. None is lost. 2 + 1 = 3. The stall opens.

Show learning afresh. Use the workbook page "Try afresh on your own", or your exercise book. Join one counter and three counters. Record the number sentence. Then join one, two and two counters. Record the number sentence.
Explain how you know both sides of each equals sign have the same value.

TB10 / WB6-7: RECALL first new word is the next number after held start; zero adds none; count-all checks. HELP 2+1=3 (say 3); RECHECK 3+2=5 (4,5), then count all 5.
TB11 / WB7: STORY 8+5=13, count 9..13; all 13 original counters conserved. The printed pictures are a model of the same inventory, not extra counters.

TB12 / WB8: FRESH-TWO 5+7=12 (6..12); FRESH-THREE 2+0+9=11 (still 2, then 3..11); FRESH-CHECK 6+3=9, claim 8 is false;7,8,9 and all 9. Equals means same value on both sides. Accept counters, dots and oral explanations, with accurate totals.

Suggested teaching: distribute TB2-7 over short sessions with movement and turns. If the held number is counted again, use TB10 two-plus-one intervention and different three-plus-two recheck. If a third set is missed, keep it separate until its turn. For zero, point to an empty space and move no object. Do not introduce column addition or counting beyond 18 here.

DELAYED next session: Cover earlier answers. Privately give six counters and five more: 11. Then three, zero and seven: 10. Ask whether 7+2=8 is true: no, correct 9. Ask the child to count on and then check all. Record independence/support. Read aloud and accept pointing, speech or seated action.

elements.text: Remember without looking back. What number do you say for the first new counter? What happens when you add zero? How do you check a sum?
Need help? Put out two counters. Count them: two. Keep two. Touch one new counter and say three. Two plus one equals three. Count all to check.
New try. Start with three counters. Add two more. Count on, then check by counting all. Use the workbook page "A smaller step", or your exercise book.
If you forget the third amount, place its counters in a separate space. Join one set at a time. If zero puzzles you, point to the empty space and move nothing.

page_text.title: Support, checks and delayed recall
page_text.subtitle: Read together. Adult guidance and answers.

elements.text:
TB10 / WB6: RECALL tens under tens, ones under ones; add ones then tens; check by joining and counting all unbundled strips. HELP 10+2=12; RECHECK 10+4=14. Use a different fresh recheck after any extra demonstration.
TB11 STORY / WB4 Q5: 22+11=33 pencils; three tens and three ones. Original stock is conserved; practice strips are separate.

TB12 / WB7 fresh: FRESH-TWO 24+13=37 (7 ones,3 tens). FRESH-ZERO 20+20=40 (0 ones,4 tens). FRESH-CHECK 12+5=17, not 62; align the 5 under the 2 as ones, not under the 1 as tens. EXPLAIN: ones totals 7,0,7 are below ten, so no new bundle. Independent all-ones checks give 37,40,17.

Suggested sessions and misconceptions: teach TB2-4, then TB5-7, then TB8-12 in several short sessions. Give all four children turns. If 5 is placed in tens, physically put five loose strips in ones. If 40 becomes 4, contrast four loose strips with four actual bundles. If needed return to TB10, then its fresh 10+4 recheck.

DELAYED next session: Cover all earlier printed and handwritten answers. Give 13+16 (29), 20+10 (30), then the claim 21+7=91 (false:28). Ask for aligned recording and a build/join/count-all check. Record independence and support.

page_text.title: Zero holds a place
page_text.subtitle: Read together. Say, point or use your workbook or exercise book.

elements.text: Mr Aliyu: Thirty has three tens and zero ones. Ten has one ten and zero ones. Zero tells us that the ones place is empty.
Tens
Ones

0 + 0 = 0 ones. 3 tens + 1 ten = 4 tens.
30 + 10 = 40. No loose ones.
Build it with four bundles. Untie and count all 40 strips to check. Keep the zero when you write 40: four means four ones; forty means four tens.
Try together: build 20 and 13. Join the tens and ones. Say why the total is 33.

elements.text:
TB9/WB5 RECALL: take away; first backward step follows the start; remaining + removed = start. SMALL-HELP 3−1=2, 2+1=3. SMALL-RECHECK 5−2=3, 3+2=5. TB10/WB5 CROSS-HELP: 11−2=9, 9+2=11. CROSS-RECHECK 11−3=8, 8+3=11.
TB11 STORY: 12−3=9 pieces on mat; 3 on tray; 9+3=12.

Teach in short sessions: TB2-4 within nine, TB5-6 crossing ten, TB7-12 checking and independence. If pupils count the start as a backward step, move one counter first, then say the number left. If they count removed counters, use separate labelled spaces. Empty the remaining space to teach zero. Never hide or discard removed objects.
DELAYED next session: Cover all answers. Independently solve 7−4=3 and 16−8=8; check 13−4=9 by 9+4=13. Ask for practical checks (3+4=7, 8+8=16). Record support and independence.
